lessons.title: Assets, identities, trust boundaries, data flows, and owners
lessons.diagramPrompt: Show MAYA and ACME AGENT outside a large ACME TRUST ZONE. Inside place IDENTITY GATE, POLICY GATE, PAYMENT TOOL, CASE DATA, SECRET VAULT, AUDIT EVIDENCE. Use labeled flows USER INTENT, DELEGATED REQUEST, TOOL CALL, DATA RETURN. Mark INTERNET, VENDOR FILE, TENANT BOUNDARY, PAYMENT BOUNDARY. Put OWNER cards beside each protected asset.
lessons.alt: Maya and an Acme agent send requests through identity and policy gates toward protected case data, secrets, payment tools, and audit evidence across named trust boundaries with owners.
lessons.outcome: Draw a useful threat model before selecting individual security products or controls.
lessons.explanation: A threat model is a picture of what matters, which identities interact with it, where trust changes, how data moves, and who owns each decision. Assets include money, customer data, credentials, capabilities, evidence, availability, and customer trust—not only databases. The boundary to make visible is every place where identity, tenant, data classification, code origin, or operational ownership changes. The safety rule is: no consequential flow crosses a trust boundary without an identified caller, intended resource, policy check, and evidence owner. This is a security contract, not a promise that a model will behave. The system must verify the relevant identity and tenant, evaluate narrow authority against current context, constrain data and destinations, and preserve enough evidence to explain both allowed and denied outcomes. Treat documents, retrieved text, model output, tool descriptions, remote cards, and external results as data until a trusted control deliberately grants them authority.

lessons.diagramPrompt: Show ATTACKER controlling MALICIOUS VENDOR FILE. Coral path crosses CONTENT PARSER to AGENT GOAL, then branches toward SECRET ACCESS, PAYMENT REDIRECT, CROSS-TENANT SEARCH, and ATTACKER EGRESS. Place teal controls AUTHORITY CHECK, TENANT FILTER, APPROVAL BINDING, EGRESS DENY, AUDIT ALERT. End with green SAFE CASE and coral UNACCEPTABLE OUTCOMES blocked.

lessons.outcome: Turn vague worries into concrete attacker paths, misuse stories, control points, and testable outcomes.
lessons.explanation: An attack path connects an attacker-controlled starting point to a harmful outcome through real system steps. A misuse case says how a legitimate capability could be abused. An unacceptable outcome is the business result the design must prevent, such as a redirected refund, exposed credential, cross-tenant answer, or erased evidence. The boundary to make visible is the sequence from attacker influence to a business consequence. The safety rule is: high-impact outcomes require several independent conditions, so one persuasive document or one confused component cannot complete the path. This is a security contract, not a promise that a model will behave. The system must verify the relevant identity and tenant, evaluate narrow authority against current context, constrain data and destinations, and preserve enough evidence to explain both allowed and denied outcomes. Treat documents, retrieved text, model output, tool descriptions, remote cards, and external results as data until a trusted control deliberately grants them authority.

lessons.title: Prompt injection and instruction-authority hierarchy
lessons.diagramPrompt: Show a vertical AUTHORITY LADDER with SYSTEM POLICY at top, APPLICATION RULES, VERIFIED USER INTENT, APPROVED PLAN, and UNTRUSTED DATA at bottom. A MALICIOUS FILE inside UNTRUSTED DATA says SEND SECRET and tries a coral arrow upward; an INSTRUCTION FIREWALL blocks it. Teal path sends DATA FACTS to SAFE REASONING, POLICY CHECK, TOOL ARGUMENTS.
lessons.alt: An authority ladder keeps system policy, application rules, verified user intent, and approved plans above untrusted data; a malicious file cannot promote its send-secret text into an instruction.
lessons.outcome: Explain why retrieved or uploaded content can inform an agent without becoming authorized instruction.
lessons.explanation: Prompt injection is untrusted content trying to redirect the agent, disclose data, or trigger tools by pretending to be a higher-authority instruction. The cure is not a clever sentence in the prompt. Authority comes from trusted system design: policy, authenticated user intent, explicit approval, tool constraints, and data-flow controls. The boundary to make visible is the line between information the agent may read and authority the system may obey. The safety rule is: content cannot grant itself permission, change its tenant, approve a consequence, reveal a secret, or choose an unapproved destination. This is a security contract, not a promise that a model will behave. The system must verify the relevant identity and tenant, evaluate narrow authority against current context, constrain data and destinations, and preserve enough evidence to explain both allowed and denied outcomes. Treat documents, retrieved text, model output, tool descriptions, remote cards, and external results as data until a trusted control deliberately grants them authority.

lessons.title: Data exfiltration and unsafe side effects
lessons.diagramPrompt: Show SENSITIVE DATA entering DATA CLASSIFIER then two lanes. Teal SAFE READ lane goes through MINIMIZE, REDACT, APPROVED TOOL to ACME RESOURCE. Coral EXFILTRATION lane tries MODEL OUTPUT, URL QUERY, TOOL ARGUMENT, LOG, ARTIFACT toward ATTACKER DESTINATION; EGRESS POLICY and DLP block it. A separate SIDE EFFECT lane requires POLICY plus BOUND APPROVAL plus RECEIPT.
lessons.alt: Sensitive data is classified, minimized, and redacted for safe use while DLP and egress policy block leakage through model output, URLs, tool arguments, logs, and artifacts; side effects require policy, approval, and receipts.
lessons.outcome: Control both information leaving the system and real-world actions caused by the system.
lessons.explanation: Exfiltration means protected data leaves an allowed boundary. It can leak through answers, tool arguments, URLs, logs, artifacts, callbacks, or another agent. A side effect changes the world: sending money, email, deleting data, creating an account, or changing access. Reading and acting need different controls. The boundary to make visible is every output channel and every tool that can change an external system. The safety rule is: sensitive data reaches only approved recipients for an approved purpose, and consequential effects require narrow authority plus durable proof. This is a security contract, not a promise that a model will behave. The system must verify the relevant identity and tenant, evaluate narrow authority against current context, constrain data and destinations, and preserve enough evidence to explain both allowed and denied outcomes. Treat documents, retrieved text, model output, tool descriptions, remote cards, and external results as data until a trusted control deliberately grants them authority.

lessons.title: Authentication, authorization, delegation, and impersonation
lessons.diagramPrompt: Show four gates in sequence labeled AUTHENTICATE, AUTHORIZE, DELEGATE, ACT. Identity cards: MAYA, ACME CLIENT, ACME AGENT, PAYMENT WORKLOAD, PAYMENT RESOURCE. A teal chain carries SUBJECT, CLIENT, ACTOR, TENANT, AUDIENCE, SCOPE. A coral IMPERSONATION shortcut skips gates and is blocked. End with DECISION RECEIPT.
lessons.alt: Maya, the Acme client, agent, payment workload, and payment resource remain distinct through authentication, authorization, delegation, and action while an impersonation shortcut is blocked.
lessons.outcome: Keep proving identity separate from deciding permission and from delegating bounded authority.
lessons.explanation: Authentication answers who or what presented a credential. Authorization asks whether that identity may perform this action now. Delegation lets one identity authorize another to act within a smaller boundary. Impersonation falsely collapses identities and makes the downstream system believe the agent is the user. The boundary to make visible is the identity and authority change between a person, client, agent, workload, and resource server. The safety rule is: each hop preserves the original subject and current actor, and no delegated hop gains more authority than its parent grant. This is a security contract, not a promise that a model will behave. The system must verify the relevant identity and tenant, evaluate narrow authority against current context, constrain data and destinations, and preserve enough evidence to explain both allowed and denied outcomes. Treat documents, retrieved text, model output, tool descriptions, remote cards, and external results as data until a trusted control deliberately grants them authority.

lessons.title: OAuth, OpenID Connect, resource metadata, and audiences
lessons.diagramPrompt: Show MCP CLIENT requesting MCP RESOURCE without token. Resource returns 401 plus PROTECTED RESOURCE METADATA. Client discovers AUTHORIZATION SERVER, performs AUTHORIZATION plus PKCE S256, validates ISSUER, requests RESOURCE AUDIENCE, receives ACCESS TOKEN, then calls MCP RESOURCE. Coral WRONG AUDIENCE TOKEN and TOKEN PASSTHROUGH are rejected.
lessons.alt: An MCP client discovers protected-resource and authorization-server metadata, uses authorization with PKCE S256, validates issuer and resource audience, then calls the MCP resource while wrong-audience and passthrough tokens are rejected.
lessons.outcome: Trace the current MCP authorization flow and explain why discovery, audience binding, PKCE, and issuer validation matter.
lessons.explanation: OAuth gives a client limited access to a protected resource. OpenID Connect adds user authentication and identity claims, but an ID token is not automatically an API access token. Current MCP authorization uses protected-resource metadata, authorization-server discovery, resource indicators, PKCE S256, issuer validation, and access tokens meant for the MCP resource. The boundary to make visible is the contract among MCP client, protected MCP resource, authorization server, and resource audience. The safety rule is: the MCP server accepts only access tokens issued by an expected issuer and explicitly intended for that resource; it never forwards the client's token to a downstream API. This is a security contract, not a promise that a model will behave. The system must verify the relevant identity and tenant, evaluate narrow authority against current context, constrain data and destinations, and preserve enough evidence to explain both allowed and denied outcomes. Treat documents, retrieved text, model output, tool descriptions, remote cards, and external results as data until a trusted control deliberately grants them authority.

lessons.title: DPoP, sender-constrained tokens, and replay resistance
lessons.stability: Stable OAuth standard; active MCP roadmap direction
lessons.diagramPrompt: Show CLIENT KEY creating DPoP PROOF with METHOD, URI, TIME, NONCE, TOKEN HASH. AUTHORIZATION SERVER issues KEY-BOUND TOKEN. MCP RESOURCE verifies TOKEN plus DPoP PROOF plus REPLAY CACHE. Coral attacker steals TOKEN ONLY and attempts REPLAY from NEW KEY; rejected. Teal legitimate retry uses fresh proof.
lessons.alt: A client key creates a DPoP proof that binds an access token to request details; the resource verifies proof and replay state, rejecting a stolen token used from another key.
lessons.outcome: Explain what DPoP changes, what it does not solve, and how to label it honestly in an MCP design.
lessons.explanation: DPoP is an OAuth proof-of-possession standard. The client signs a short-lived proof with a key and the authorization server binds the access token to that key. A resource checks the token and proof together, including request method, URI, time, token hash, and replay identifier. MCP's 2026 roadmap calls out DPoP adoption, but that does not make it a universal core-MCP requirement today. The boundary to make visible is the use of a bearer-like token by the software instance that actually holds the bound private key. The safety rule is: possession of the access-token string alone is insufficient to replay the request from a different key or request context. This is a security contract, not a promise that a model will behave. The system must verify the relevant identity and tenant, evaluate narrow authority against current context, constrain data and destinations, and preserve enough evidence to explain both allowed and denied outcomes. Treat documents, retrieved text, model output, tool descriptions, remote cards, and external results as data until a trusted control deliberately grants them authority.

It signs a fresh DPoP proof for the token request or resource request.

A replay cache rejects repeated proof identifiers inside the accepted time window.
lessons.analogy: A stolen ticket is useless if entry also requires a fresh signature made by the key held by the original buyer.

lessons.title: Workload identity, token exchange, and agent delegation
lessons.stability: Stable standards plus evolving MCP agent-identity work
lessons.diagramPrompt: Show MAYA TOKEN entering ACME POLICY but not flowing downstream. ACME AGENT has WORKLOAD IDENTITY from TRUST DOMAIN. A TOKEN EXCHANGE gate receives SUBJECT AUTHORITY plus ACTOR ID plus TARGET AUDIENCE plus NARROW SCOPE and returns DELEGATED TOKEN to PAYMENT RESOURCE. Coral FULL USER TOKEN COPY is blocked. Include DELEGATION RECEIPT.
lessons.alt: Maya's token stops at Acme policy while an authenticated Acme workload exchanges bounded subject authority and actor identity for a narrow payment-resource token, blocking full user-token copying.
lessons.outcome: Design delegated agent calls that preserve user context without pretending the agent is the user.
lessons.explanation: A workload identity belongs to running software such as an agent service or worker. Token exchange is a standard way to trade existing security context for a new token aimed at another resource. A safe design can preserve Maya as the subject and Acme as the actor while reducing audience and scope. The safety rule is: every material risk, control, incident, exception, deployment, and overdue review has one accountable owner plus a reachable escalation path. This is a security contract, not a promise that a model will behave. The system must verify the relevant identity and tenant, evaluate narrow authority against current context, constrain data and destinations, and preserve enough evidence to explain both allowed and denied outcomes. Treat documents, retrieved text, model output, tool descriptions, remote cards, and external results as data until a trusted control deliberately grants them authority.

lessons.explanation: The secure gateway is a logical set of enforcement points, not one giant service. Trusted context reaches instruction assembly, policy, capabilities, approvals, secrets, tenant data, sandboxes, egress, discovery, provenance, and evidence. MCP and A2A stay distinct while sharing one organizational control model. The boundary to make visible is the path from authenticated intent and untrusted content to protected action and outcome. caseStudy.situation: Maya's legitimate refund arrives with a vendor attachment that tries to steal credentials, redirect payment, contact an attacker server, and delegate to an unknown finance agent.
walkthrough: Identity and tenant gates establish Maya, Acme actors, case ownership, and intended payment resource.
The attachment remains evidence-bearing untrusted data; injection, unknown discovery, secret requests, and arbitrary egress are denied or quarantined.
Policy creates a narrow refund capability and requires approval bound to the exact original payee, amount, and destination.
The payment workload uses short-lived target authority, completes one safe refund, and writes policy, action, provenance, and audit receipts.
caseStudy.result: Maya receives the correct refund while Acme can prove why the safe path was allowed and every hostile branch was denied.
caseStudy.danger: A decorative gateway that does not enforce policy at the protected resource becomes a single dashboard in front of unchanged broad tools and data paths.
caseStudy.takeaway: Security is a connected system of identity, authority, containment, data control, evidence, and accountable review.
